issues.legal_issue: Inherent powers cannot be used to set aside a decree when the governing procedure expressly provides a remedy for setting it aside and the requirements for that remedy are not met.
material_facts: The tenant applied to set aside an ejectment decree under the specific procedure governing the suit.
That procedure expressly empowered the court to set aside such a decree in specified circumstances.
The courts found that the circumstances required for setting aside the decree under that procedure did not exist.
issues.conclusion: The court could not use its inherent powers to set aside the decree when the application did not satisfy the express remedy provided by the governing procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, inherent powers are exercised only in very exceptional circumstances for which the Code lays down no procedure. Where Order 37, rule 4 expressly provides for setting aside a decree, section 151 cannot be used to bypass that provision when its requirements are not met. The court relied on Manohar Lal v. Seth Hiralal.

predicates.set_aside_application_under_specific_pro: A party applied to set aside a decree under the specific procedure governing the proceeding.
predicates.procedure_expressly_provides_set_aside_p: The procedure governing the proceeding expressly provides a power to set aside the decree.
predicates.required_set_aside_circumstances_absent: The court found that the circumstances required to set aside the decree under that procedure were absent.

issues.definition: When a party seeks to set aside a decree under a procedure that expressly provides for that relief, and the required circumstances are absent, the court cannot use inherent power to set aside the decree.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal arising from an application under a procedure cannot provide relief on the ground that the procedure was inapplicable when that ground would make the underlying application incompetent.
material_facts: The tenant's appeal arose from an application to set aside the decree under the procedure used to hear the ejectment suit.
The tenant argued in the appeal that the procedure was inapplicable to the suit.
If that argument were accepted, the application made under that procedure would itself be incompetent.
The tenant had used that procedure and had consented to an order made within it.
issues.conclusion: No relief could be granted in this appeal on the contention that the procedure was inapplicable; accepting the contention would make the tenant's application incompetent, and any challenge to the decree required other appropriate proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: The court held that the procedural posture of the appeal limited the relief available: an appeal from the disposition of an application under a procedure could not be used to grant relief on a contention that would render that application incompetent. It also noted that the tenant had invoked the procedure and consented to an order under it.

predicates.appeal_arises_from_application_under_cha: The appeal arises from the disposition of an application made under the procedure whose applicability is challenged.
predicates.appellant_claims_procedure_inapplicable: The appellant argues that the procedure used in the underlying proceeding did not apply.
predicates.accepting_claim_would_make_application_i: If the appellant's argument were accepted, the application from which the appeal arose would be incompetent.

issues.definition: When an appeal arises from an application made under a challenged procedure, and accepting the challenge would make that application incompetent, the appeal cannot grant relief on that ground.

issues.legal_issue: A procedure deeming pleading allegations admitted after leave to defend is denied does not require a decree regardless of whether the plaintiff is legally entitled to one.
material_facts: The ejectment suit proceeded under a procedure that treated the plaint's allegations as admitted when the tenant had no leave to defend.
The tenant lost the leave to defend after failing to comply with the payment condition attached to it.
The governing law could require the court to exercise discretion on the facts deemed admitted.
issues.conclusion: The court had to accept the plaint's allegations as correct but still apply the law, including any required discretion, and could decree only the relief to which the plaintiff was legally entitled.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 37, rule 2, the effect of the defendant's failure to obtain leave to defend is that the plaint's allegations are deemed admitted. The court must nevertheless apply the law to those allegations: it cannot grant relief where the plaint discloses no cause of action, and it must exercise any discretion that the governing law requires on the admitted facts.

predicates.summary_procedure_decree_after_leave_den: A claim for a decree proceeds under a summary procedure after the defendant has been denied leave to defend.
predicates.pleading_allegations_deemed_admitted: The procedure treats the allegations in the pleading as admitted because the defendant has no leave to defend.
predicates.governing_law_requires_discretion: The law governing the claim requires the court to exercise discretion on the facts treated as admitted.

issues.definition: When a summary procedure treats pleading allegations as admitted after leave to defend is denied, the court must still apply the governing law and exercise any discretion that law requires before granting a decree.

issues.legal_issue: A procedural rule applying a summary procedure to statutory eviction suits is not invalid merely because a defendant must follow that procedure to present a defence.
material_facts: A rule made under the rent-control legislation applied the summary procedure to suits for possession by landlords against tenants.
Under that procedure, the tenant could lose the opportunity to defend by failing to comply with its requirements.
The court could still apply the governing law to the allegations deemed admitted, including any discretion required by that law.
The tenant argued that the procedure conflicted with the rent-control legislation because the court had discretion over whether to grant possession.
issues.conclusion: The rule applying the summary procedure was not ultra vires; prescribing a procedure for exercising statutory rights did not create a conflict with the legislation merely because a party had to comply with that procedure to be heard.
issues.legal_principle: Section 49 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947 empowered the government to make rules to give effect to the Act, and rule 8 applied Order 37 to the relevant suits. The court held that procedural rules may prescribe how rights are exercised and are not ultra vires solely because compliance with the procedure is required. Order 37 does not require a decree contrary to law: the court applies the law, including any discretion required on the admitted facts.

predicates.statutory_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks to enforce a statutory right to possession through an eviction suit.
predicates.rule_prescribes_procedure_for_exercising: A rule prescribes the procedure a party must follow to exercise or defend against the statutory right.
predicates.procedure_preserves_governing_legal_test: The court remains able to apply the governing legal requirements, including any required discretion, despite the prescribed procedure.

issues.definition: A rule prescribing how parties must exercise or defend against a statutory right is not invalid merely for regulating that process when the court can still apply the governing legal test.
